extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, poets and critics interested in epic poetry (readers of The Spectator / commentators on Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic poetry (exemplified by commentary on Milton's Paradise Lost): character-voice, use of the marvellous, unity of action, invocation and devotional imagery, dream-scenes, and the elevation of domestic subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing the reader for occurrences / judicious foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Author, who shews a wonderful Art throughout his whole Poem, in preparing the Reader for the several Occurrences that arise in it, founds upon the above-mention'd Circumstance ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreshadow events artfully so that later occurrences feel founded and natural; prepare the reader with antecedent circumstances without flatly telling the outcome or spoiling the narrative. The critic praises Milton for this kind of preparation as part of poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of character speech; avoid ill-fitting flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: “An injudicious Poet would have made Adam talk thro the whole Work in such Sentiments as these: But Flattery and Falshood are not the Courtship of Milton's Adam…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a character's speech consistent with his moral and cognitive state; avoid extravagant flattery or false sentiments that would be implausible in a character (e.g., Adam in Innocence). If such speech is used, motivate it (Milton uses it only in a dream produced to taint Eve's imagination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-scenes should exhibit natural wildness and inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: “tho the Vision it self is founded upon Truth, the Circumstances of it are full of that Wildness and Inconsistency which are natural to a Dream.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using dreams as a poetic device, preserve the dream-like qualities (wildness, inconsistency) so the scene reads as a genuine dream and serves its rhetorical purpose (e.g., foreshadowing or corrupting imagination) without becoming an ordinary rational speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocations of nature in hymns — proper for devotional effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Morning Hymn is written in Imitation of one of those Psalms... Invocations of this nature fill the Mind with glorious Ideas of God's Works, and awaken that Divine Enthusiasm...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calling upon inanimate parts of creation in devotional poetry can legitimately inspire awe and devotion; such invocations are especially fitting for primeval or devotional contexts (e.g., first parents) and should produce an uplifting, pious tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify marvellous elements by authoritative parallels (Scripture/Homer)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Poet here seems to have regarded two or three Passages in the 18th Iliad... I will not pretend to determine, whether in this particular of Homer the Marvellous does not lose sight of the Probable. As the miraculous Workmanship of Milton's Gates is not so extraordinary as this of the Tripodes, so I am persuaded he would not have mentioned it, had not he been supported in it by a Passage in the Scripture...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating marvellous or supernatural imagery is permissible when supported by authoritative parallels (Scripture, classical models) or when it remains within probable bounds; such support lends plausibility and grounding to the marvellous in epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the marvellous with the probable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Scaliger has rallied Homer very severely upon this Point... whether in this particular of Homer the Marvellous does not lose sight of the Probable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow marvellous wonders to undermine plausibility; the marvellous should be handled with restraint so it enhances wonder without lapsing into the implausible or absurd. Compare and temper marvels against accepted authorities or scriptural precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions of supernatural beings should conform to scriptural notions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I do not remember to have met with any so finely drawn, and so conformable to the Notions which are given of them in Scripture, as this in Milton.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting angels or other theological beings, align description with canonical/scriptural conceptions to achieve resonance and authority; fine poetic detail that remains consonant with religious notions is commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate domestic or low subject-matter with pleasing images and strong expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “Though in this, and other Parts of the same Book, the Subject is only the Housewifry of our first Parent, it is set off with so many pleasing Images and strong Expressions, as make it none of the least agreeable Parts in this Divine Work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common, domestic activities can be made poetically significant by richly imagined description and forceful diction; do not dismiss humble subjects — they can yield fine poetic passages when adorned with apt imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve unity of action in epic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whichever of the Notions be true, the Unity of Milton's Action is preserved according to either of them; whether we consider the Fall of Man in its immediate Beginning... or in its more remote Beginning...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a coherent unity of action even if episodes may be interpreted as having different commencements; episodic material should not violate the overall dramatic unity of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary characters as moral patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Part of Abdiel... exhibits to us a noble Moral of religious Singularity... The Author doubtless designed it as a Pattern to those who live among Mankind...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include characters whose actions model virtues (e.g., loyalty, constancy) to instruct and inspire readers; heroic exemplars serve both literary and moral ends in epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character behavior must match dignity and role
rubrics_metrics.description: “Raphael's Behaviour is every way suitable to the Dignity of his Nature, and to that Character of a sociable Spirit... he is represented as sitting down at Table with Adam, and eating of the Fruits of Paradise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters (even supernatural ones) acting in ways consistent with their established dignity and social role; small actions and manners (e.g., Raphael dining sociably) should cohere with characterization and serve the poem's moral and rhetorical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic imitation should be judicious and illuminating
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think there is no question but the Poet in the Conferences between Adam and Eve, had his Eye very frequently upon the Book of Canticles... Milton had his Eye very frequently upon the Book of Canticles... I think there is no question but the Poet... remember'd those two Passages...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of earlier models (Biblical, classical) is effective when it is judicious and serves to illuminate the present work; echoes and parallels should enrich meaning rather than appear slavish or irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artless simplicity is an amiable quality in personal letters
rubrics_metrics.description: “how amiable Ignorance may be when it is shewn in its Simplicities... an honest Countryman to his Mistress... kept... as an Image of artless Love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In personal correspondence and simple narrative voices, preserve naturalness and plainness; unpolished, sincere expression can be charming and valued as authentic, especially in epistolary or anecdotal material.
